Broken Promises KZN
In the KZN Broken Promises trilogy we will be looking at the following projects.
On landing at King Shaka Airport Lourensa will discover the history behind the new landmark.

1. DURBAN

King Shaka Airport Statue

The reason for including this in the programme is that it acts as a metaphor for many of the projects that have been commissioned in KZN.

Newspaper reports say that it will be unveiled on the 27th of April by the new Zulu King.

When the airport opened in 2010 a statue of King Shaka was unveiled. Depicted as a cow herd with three Nguni cows around him. There was a public outcry that King Shaka was depicted as a lowly cowherd and not as warrior king, many felt that it was demeaning. The statue of cow herd Shaka removed and is apparently in Dube Trade Port somewhere. ( I am hoping to find where it is and film it.)
A new sculpture was commissioned and it was completed by 2018. But it took nearly 6 years to get the statue to the airport. It is still covered in burlap at the airport. Waiting for Royal family approval.
Like many tenders in KZN pay double for start of project and someone to finish abandoned project abandoned project.

Original Statue Without Shaka



New Statue. Actually it doesn’t look like this there is scaffolding around it and shade cloth that is flapping in the wind.

More sculpture info
In 2019 Carte Blanche made a programme about Lungelo Gumede who was commissioned to make two sculptures of President Nelson Mandela and Oliver Tambo.
https://www.iol.co.za/ios/news/city-mum-on-statues-made-in-china-be38359a-07d7-4fa2-8af6-c9c6f9a5a63d
2022 8 October Last Friday, the Independent on Saturday reported that the two statues of former president Nelson Mandela and former ANC president Oliver Tambo were on their way to being immortalised in bronze for a handsome, already paid-up sum.
“Both statues cost roughly R22m,” municipal spokesperson Msawakhe Mayisela told our sister paper The Mercury.
“This was the cheapest figure as compared to others who wanted about the same price for only one statue.”
Action: I will go and see if I can find Lungelo and ask him what has happened to his sculptures.
Need someone to give perspective on doing things twice in KZN.






2. UMVOTI Bridge

Contact Ground UP Nokulunga Majola
https://groundup.org.za/article/r66-million-bridge-left-air/
The foundations for the Umdloti Bridge, a R65.7 million project, have been left untouched since October 2018.
Residents of Ogunjini in Verulam, north of Durban, say the project had created jobs for many people in the area and they are disappointed it came to a halt.
Sindisiwe Zondi said the current crossing gets flooded. “You risk drowning. Even vehicles cannot cross …. Children cannot go to school, ” she said.
Nana Mthembu said she almost drowned once on the old causeway. “There are no barricades to protect people when a speeding vehicle passes … I think it was built as a temporary solution in the first place. We were hoping that the new bridge would be safer.”
“Many of our brothers and sisters lost their jobs when the project was stopped and most of them are still unemployed. It’s been over two years and still we don’t know what happened,” said Mthembu.
“We are hoping that when the project resumes they will do the right thing and employ people from the community,” said Thulani Gama, who had worked on the project. He hasn’t had any luck finding another job.
According to the KwaZulu-Natal Department of Transport, the contractor could not meet the contract specifications and this led to a breach of contract.
“Due to no progress on site despite the departmental intervention, the contract was terminated,” said spokesperson Kwanele Ncalane.
He said the department was busy finalising specifications and would re-advertise the contract for another supplier to complete the works on site.
“The process normally takes approximately six months for the contract to be awarded and another 42 days to get the Construction Work Permit so that the contractor can start construction,” he said.
Ncalane said once construction commenced, work on the bridge was expected to take 12 months.
The original contractor was Tekewini Civils CC. GroundUp managed to reach them but they have not responded to our questions.

KZN's 'bridge of tragedy' to be completed. KwaZulu-Natal transport department will complete the infamous bridge connecting eThekwini and Ndwedwe, seven years after it was started. In the photo below one can see the 3 pillars that were built and abandoned.
Construction of the Ogunjini/Umvoti River bridge began in 2016 but was abandoned in 2019 — with only three concrete pillars erected — by the contractor who cited financial constraints. The bridge was meant to replace the old, low-lying bridge the community of Ogunjini used to cross the Umvoti River.
KZN MEC for transport, community safety and liaison Sipho Hlomuka was among those present during a sod turning ceremony for the R79m Umdloti/Ogunjini River bridge. This bridge connects eThekwini metro and Ndwedwe.
“There were court processes ... and we had to wait until the end of that contract before we could start finding a new contractor,” said Ndwedwe mayor Simon Mfeka.
The low bridge put residents at risk of being swept away after heavy rain and at least three people have died since the project was halted four years ago.

On Tuesday, KZN transport MEC Sipho Hlomuka launched the construction of the new bridge and introduced the new contractor, WSM Group, to the community.
“We are on the bridge that has been sweeping away our people. We have come to unveil the new contractor who will start working from today [Tuesday]. The bridge is the link between Ndwedwe and the eThekwini metro. We're hopeful that this time the project will be completed,” said Hlomuka.
“We have a contractor we trust and have seen complete their work before and on time. That gives us confidence, but they cannot do it without the co-operation of the community. The completion of this project will depend on many different stakeholders. The councillors and traditional leadership have committed to ensuring a smooth completion of the project.”
The bridge was damaged in the floods last year in an incident that saw an eThekwini municipality vehicle trying to cross it being swept away with two workers inside.

The bodies of the workers were found three days later, a few metres from the car they were travelling in.
“This bridge has a long history, but it is not a good one because people lost their lives while trying to cross this bridge. Fixing it evokes many thoughts within us and the families who lost their loved ones here. This work is a sign to respect those who lost their lives here,” said eThekwini council speaker Thabani Nyawose.
The bodies of other people who were swept away haven’t been found, according to eThekwini ward 59 councillor Nkosiyesizwe Mhlongo.
Mfeka said the community was also responsible, as they damaged it during a service delivery protest. He said it first collapsed while a water tanker was trying to cross it to deliver water to the community and “that’s where the problems started”.

https://www.timeslive.co.za/news/south-africa/2023-03-15-kzns-bridge-of-tragedy-to-be-completed/
Action: Go to the river. See if new work started. Also try and find family of deceased.

3.OTHONGATI - Eleven houses built for R 87 million

The housing project was launched in 2017 at Umbhayi informal settlement 248 units were meant to be built, however, only 11 units have been built in the last six years with a price tag of a staggering R87 million.
There has been no progress on the huge Umbhayi housing development in Tongaat, north of Durban, since the contractor left the site in 2021.
Families moved off the land to make way for the development are still living in a transit camp, without proper sanitation or electricity.
Several children have died as a result of illegal (izinyoka) electricity connections.
The eThekwini municipality says a new contractor will be appointed before October this year but has not given reasons for the delay.
In 2019, more than 200 families from Umbhayi informal settlement in Tongaat, north of Durban, were moved to a transit camp to make way for an RDP housing project about half a km away. Four years later, not a single house has been finished. Meanwhile the families live in zinc houses, with broken communal toilets. Many houses do not have electricity and izinyoka connections have caused many deaths.

R130 million RDP housing project in the eThekwini Metropolitan Municipality that started in 2017 remains incomplete. Over 800 families were expected to benefit from the Umbhayi Project. Only 11 units were completed in the last six years and remain unoccupied.
The 11 complete units have already been vandalised. Seven further units lack roofs. About a kilometre away from the Umbhayi Project is a transit camp. People here were promised they would be moved into the RDP housing project.
To further exacerbate the housing crisis in the area, across the road lies an informal settlement.
At the transit camp, families live in houses made of corrugated iron. They are forced to relieve themselves in the nearby bushes, faced with blocked and broken communal toilets and showers.
Several illegal electricity connections are visible.
Fifty-one-year-old Nokuthula Mthethwa lives here. She uses crutches after suffering a stroke last year.
She says, “This housing issue is such a big problem; we are waiting and unsure of when this project will resume. Nobody has been in touch with us to let us know what the issue is with this housing project. We are presently waiting, but even the ones we are currently living in are not in good condition. They don’t even have doors, which is extremely frustrating to me since I am unemployed. Maybe it’s better for those who are employed, but for me, it’s worse since I am using a walking stick because I have a stroke diagnosis. I hope they can also help us with electricity connections.”
The community says the incomplete units at the housing project are also being used as a hideout for criminals. Another land allocated for more housing units is filled with overgrown grass.
Linda Chetty says she has lost hope of getting her RDP house.
“We really did lose hope now because it’s like we are just left in a lurch to make believe we are going to get those houses, but I don’t think so because if you look at the community now. It’s getting bigger and bigger, with more and more houses coming up all over. So, I don’t know; it’s like there is no hope. For the years, we’ve lived in the community, it’s like some of them have also been deceased, like we have belief and hope that we’re going to get a house this year.”
Sindi Mngoma lives in the nearby informal settlement. She speaks about feeling abandoned by the municipality.
“We don’t have water; we are doing laundry on one water tap that was installed a long time ago, and it’s far away from us. We don’t have toilets; we have to go to the bushes in order to relieve ourselves. We don’t have electricity; we are using candles. When you connect illicit electricity, you must pay for it as well, just like when you are using legal electricity.”
The eThekwini Municipality is aware of inquiries made by SABC News regarding the Umbhayi Housing Project, specifically related to why the project has stalled and confirmation of the allocated funds, but they have yet to respond.
4. ESHOWE

Abandoned agricultural land purchased by KZN Land Affairs

More than 21 properties in the Empangeni and Eshowe districts, and reportedly many more across KZN bought by the land affairs department, lie fallow, producing only weeds, dead trees and choked sugar cane.

Hennie de Villiers, a board member of the KZN agricultural union and chairman of the district agricultural committee in uThungulu - where more than 10 farms have been abandoned - said not only had land reform failed in the district, but it had also cost jobs and millions of rands in income from sugar cane, vegetables and export citrus.

"At least 500 farm workers have lost their jobs. On one farm alone, over R9 million a year in income from export grapefruit has been squandered. All these farms were producing at least 60 tons of sugar cane a hectare a year. Now there is nothing," said de Villiers.

On Valley Farm, Confluence, Concor and Grass Farm, valuable citrus trees are dead, irrigation pipes have been ripped from the ground and productive sugar cane fields have been either burnt or become overgrown with weeds.

On Valley Farm, Confluence, Concor and Grass Farm, valuable citrus trees are dead, irrigation pipes have been ripped from the ground and productive sugar cane fields have been either burnt or become overgrown with weeds.
De Villiers said all the farms had been handed over as working entities.
Action: Get hold of Hennie and go to Eshowe

KZN BROKEN PROMISES – Stenette & John




VO
It’s arguably the most hotly-contested of all our provinces in the coming election; a region on a knife’s edge.
With balloting less than two weeks away, now is the time to reflect on past commitments and promises broken.


PETE
I can’t think of a single promise that they have actually kept - let alone broken
LINDA
There's no hope. They don't help us.


VO
Durban, our country’s third largest city. Everywhere are signs of decay and it’s drowning in sewage.


BRONWYN
They had to actually cancel the beach events due to the sewerage in our water.


Vukhile
The municipality must fix the pipes.


VO
As the elections approach, it's a city battling to keep its head above water.




FADE TO BLACK


Aircraft land
VO
It might be a small province, but KZN is the second-biggest contributor to our economy… although the welcome at King Shaka airport arrivals suggests otherwise.


LOURENSA
These bronzed and Nguni statues do feel a bit out of place here at the airport.






VOXPOPS
It's probably something to do with, the rural, Nguni cattle or whatever
I don't know. They represent nature.
I think these cows represent, our kingdom. KZN.
They're a bit out of place, because what does that have to do with the airport's name?
VO
Unveiled amid much fanfare in 2010, the sculpture featured King Shaka Zulu himself.
President Jacob Zuma had approved the project, but the Zulu Royal Family hadn’t been consulted on the design and were apparently angry that Shaka had been depicted as a cow herder.
Less than a month later, the monarch was quietly removed.


Lourensa
It's taken 14 years to find a replacement and it now costs twice as much. The new, very impressive 12 metre statue is yet to be unveiled, and it certainly makes a statement.


VO
The Shaka statue might just as well be a monument to the significant number of other projects that are unfinished, over-budget or both.
V/O
Just a stone’s throw from the airport, a relic from the not-so-distant past…
Loursensa
In February this year, President Cyril Ramaphosa launched the ANC election manifesto to a packed out Moses Mabhida Stadium. The party's election slogan is “let's do more together.”
VO
One thing KZNs’ residents and tourists won’t be doing together, is enjoying the views from the top of that very stadium.
It featured a so-called “sky car” making it one of the more unique venues built for the 2010 soccer World Cup. But, for the past six years, it hasn’t moved an inch.
The municipality promised Moses Mabhida wouldn’t become an economic burden and would boost tourism. And for a while it did. Then the Sky Car broke and no-one fixed it.
Alan
When we asked them how come it’s not working, they blame Covid. But when we actually asked him and told him but Covid happened off to this guy, Covid stopped working. They were lost for words
VO
Alan Beesley is a local councillor and serves on the Municipal Public Accounts Committee…
Alan
If they'd repaired and maintained this over the years and still be running and the residents and businesses of Ethekwini wouldn't have to be forking out 115 million to fix this thing.
VO
In 2020 the municipality said it would cost R15 million to fix the Sky Car. Four years later, the estimated price tag is R 115 million.
When added to the overall cost of running and maintaining the stadium - less whatever money it generates in a year - the burden to the taxpayer is significant.
Alan
Currently this stadium is operating at a R220 million loss a year.
Vo
By 2014, the roughly 7 million people visiting Durban each year were spending around R19 billion. By 2022, visitor numbers dropped by around 90% to just 700,000.
Vukhile GAZU has operated his rickshaw on Durban's promenade for 15 years. His daily earnings have plummeted and he now makes barely enough to cover his bus fare home.


Vukhile
The pipes have sewage and that’s what’s going into the ocean, making people stay away.
It’s because the municipality has failed to fix the pipes.


VO
Sewage has been a problem on several Ethekwini beaches for years.


VO
Once a surfing mecca, the contamination forced the cancellation of the recent SA Championships, and businesses along the beachfront are suffering.
Bronwyn
We have sewerage coming onto our beaches from the sewerage drains and it is just never getting fixed.
VO
The stench here is overwhelming, but the state of the Umgeni River which flows into the ocean not far from the Moses Mabhida Stadium is truly shocking.
Pete
This is one of the most contaminated geographic places in Durban…20 million litres of sewerage a day is not even getting to the waste water treatment plant.
VO
Pete Graham is an environmental activist.
Pete
Let’s be very clear; the national government and the provincial government of KZN has issued a number of directives for them to clean up their act. And the city has simply refused to follow all directives.
VO
We tried contacting Ethekiwini’s Mayor, Mxolisi Kaunda… but he’s a hard man to pin down.
VO
his office did respond in writing to some of our questions, saying….
“There are many factors that led to sewer spillages, like theft and vandalism…

Natural disasters have also exacerbated the problem so it is not true that the City has failed to discharge the duty of care.”


V/O
The City is concerned about the drop in tourism in general.
Surprisingly, though, they predict a staggering 355% increase in visitors to the city this year.

VO
Away from the polluted Umgeni, just north of the airport and its yet-to-be unveiled Shaka statue lies oThongathi – formally Tongaat.


Lourensa
In 2019, the Ethekwini municipality allocated 134 million rand to build over 200 houses. Today all that has been built are these 11 partially finished units…


VO
The initial planning at the Umbhayi Housing Development was completed about 3 years ago. And since then nothing…
empty platformed terraces waiting for houses…and speed limits on deserted roads.


Linda
There’s no hope, they don’t help us, we don’t have electricity we don’t have houses
Too long, they promised the people.
VO
When construction first began, Linda Khaile and her family were promised a home here. That was six years ago.
Linda
The project they stopped. They don’t tell the people why the project stopped.
VO
Thembela Mahiloyi is a community leader. He and his family lived in a house with six rooms before it was demolished to make way for the development. He was put into this temporary accommodation along with 200 other families and told they’d have new homes within three years.
Thembela
Lourensa: So, they destroyed your houses? Yeah. To build new houses, but they haven't built anything.
Thembela: Nothing.


VO
It’s filthy here… and depressing. There’s no rubbish removal, the roofs are rusted and leak, the toilets are broken and the surrounding bush is covered in human waste.
VO
The Mayor’s statement says a new contractor would be introduced to the community and that only R 70 million has been spent on the contract so far. But there’s no indication of when the project will be finished..


Thembela
Lourensa: Do you think that this housing project will force people to vote in a different way?
Thembela: Our worry and surprise is that how come can Ethekwini municipality can do this South African people whom are voting for this in every election.






Over three weeks, we’ve visited three of our nine provinces. We’ve spoken to people who have reason to be suspicious of political promises given how many have been broken. And perhaps, more than any other time since 1994, that’s given them even more reason to vote.

*** END***


PROMOS




Promo 1
V/O
On this piece of land 248 families were promised a home to call their own.
Linda
We have no hope, we have no house.
Too long they promised us.
V/O
With a price tag of R 70 million only 11 houses have been partially completed.
What is the cost KZN’s unfulfilled promises?

Promo 2
V/O
Durban, once South Africa’s holiday mecca - now struggling to stay afloat in dirty water.
Vukile
The sewerage pipe from the Umngeni River is going straight into the sea.
That is why there are no people.
V/O
We count the cost of the broken promises in KZN.

Promo 3
V/O
Millions of litres of raw sewage running into the sea and a tourism industry on its knees.
“December holidays aren’t as busy as what it used to be.
The slew of broken promises in Kwazulu Natal.
“I can’t think of a single promise that they have actually kept - let alone broken”
